content.title: About
content.content: Pickled beets are cooked beetroot preserved in a vinegar brine with sugar, salt and spices. They have a vivid red color, a sweet‑sour flavor and a firm yet tender texture. Pickled beets are used in salads, appetizers and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pickled beets are a staple in many Eastern European dishes, such as the classic vinaigrette salad.
The bright color comes from betanin, a powerful antioxidant that remains stable during pickling.
Most of the B‑vitamins and minerals are retained after the pickling process.
There are many recipe variations, including mustard, garlic, bay leaf or juniper berry additions.
Properly sealed jars can keep pickled beets fresh for several months in the refrigerator.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Betanin helps protect cells from oxidative stress and may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in beets promotes regular bowel movements and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Pickled beets contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle function.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Pickled vegetables can be high in salt, so people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Vinegar allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to vinegar components.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Excessive consumption of acidic foods may irritate the stomach in those with gastritis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled beets can be enjoyed straight from the jar, diced into salads, added to sandwiches, soups, or served as a side to meat dishes. They are usually sliced or cubed before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the jar of pickled beets refrigerated after opening. When stored properly, they retain flavor and quality for 2–3 months. Discard if you notice mold, off‑smell, or any signs of spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Breadfruit (Artocarpus altilis) is a large tropical fruit that resembles a bread‑like texture and flavor. When cooked—by boiling, baking, or frying—it becomes soft, aromatic, and mildly sweet. The fruit is a staple in Southeast Asian, Oceanic, and Caribbean cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A single breadfruit can weigh up to 30 kg and measure over 30 cm in length.
Raw fruit is high in starch, which turns into easily digestible sugars when heated.
In traditional Oceanic cooking, breadfruit often replaces potatoes or rice.
A breadfruit tree can produce fruit for 20‑30 years with minimal decline.
Leaves and roots are used in folk medicine to treat wounds and colds.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: Cooked breadfruit provides slowly digestible starch that helps maintain satiety over time.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: One hundred grams of cooked breadfruit supplies about 15 mg of vitamin C, supporting immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids fluid balance and normal heart function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Breadfruit contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and supports a balanced gut microbiome.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to breadfruit proteins.

items.title: High starch content
items.content: Large portions can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar levels for people with diabetes.

items.title: Toxicity of unripe fruit
items.content: Raw unripe breadfruit contains cyanogenic glycosides and must be fully cooked before consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked breadfruit can be boiled in salted water, baked with herbs, pan‑fried, or added to soups and curries. It is often cubed and tossed into salads or served as a side dish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked breadfruit in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Frozen portions retain quality for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Lactose‑free whole milk is regular cow’s milk that has had the lactose sugar removed while retaining the full fat content and all the nutrients typical of whole milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lactose‑free milk is produced by adding lactase enzyme, which breaks down lactose into glucose and galactose.
Whole milk contains about 3.5 % fat, giving it a richer, creamier taste than skimmed varieties.
The product is suitable for people with lactose intolerance but tastes like regular whole milk.
In many markets it is sold in 1 L and 0.5 L cartons.
Milk is a good source of calcium, vitamin D and B‑vitamins.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Calcium supports strong bones and teeth and plays a role in muscle contraction and nerve signaling.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D enhances calcium absorption and contributes to immune health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Milk protein provides all essential amino acids needed for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: The fat in whole milk supplies energy and helps absorb fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Digestive ease for lactose‑intolerant
items.content: Added lactase makes the milk easy to digest for those who cannot process lactose.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to casein or whey proteins with allergic symptoms.

items.title: Higher calorie content
items.content: Whole milk is more calorie‑dense; people watching their weight should account for it in their diet.

items.title: Possible added sugars
items.content: Although lactose is removed, some brands may add small amounts of sugar for taste.

items.title: Shelf‑life considerations
items.content: Once opened, the milk spoils quickly and must be kept refrigerated.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink it cold, add to cereals, smoothies, baking, sauces, and desserts. It also works well in infant formulas and other child‑friendly preparations.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. After opening, consume within 5–7 days. Do not freeze, as the fat structure may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Herbalife Nutritional Powder Mix is a balanced blend of proteins, vitamins, and minerals designed to support muscle growth and post‑workout recovery. The powder dissolves easily in water, milk, or juice and has a pleasant neutral taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Contains a mix of whey and soy protein, providing both fast and sustained amino acid delivery.
One serving (30 g) delivers approximately 20 g of high‑quality protein.
Formulated with B‑vitamins, vitamin C, calcium, and iron to support overall metabolism.
The product has undergone clinical testing for safety and efficacy within Herbalife programs.
Packaged in recyclable plastic to reduce environmental impact.

items.title: Supports muscle growth
items.content: The high content of complete protein promotes muscle‑fiber synthesis after physical activity.

items.title: Accelerates recovery
items.content: Fast‑absorbing proteins and amino acids help shorten recovery time between workouts.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamins C and E, along with zinc, strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Stabilizes energy levels
items.content: B‑vitamins participate in energy metabolism, maintaining alertness throughout the day.

items.title: Strengthens bones
items.content: Calcium and vitamin D contribute to maintaining bone density.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Whey protein may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk‑protein sensitivity.

items.title: Excessive protein intake
items.content: Consuming too much protein can strain the kidneys, especially in people with pre‑existing kidney conditions.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some versions contain sucralose or aspartame, which may not be suitable for all consumers.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Calcium can reduce absorption of certain antibiotics and thyroid medications.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix one scoop (30 g) of powder with 250–300 ml of water, milk, or a plant‑based beverage. For added flavor and nutrition, blend with fruit, berries, or oats.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place with the package tightly sealed. After opening, use within 2–3 months for best quality.

content.title: About
content.content: Cream soda is a non‑alcoholic, lightly carbonated beverage with a sweet vanilla or creamy flavor. It is often used as a base for cocktails, dessert drinks, and in children's meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first cream soda recipe appeared in the United States in the late 19th century.
Its traditional color is light‑brown or creamy, achieved by adding caramel.
In some countries it is served with a scoop of ice cream – the “float”.
Typical cream soda contains little to no caffeine.
Flavor is often enhanced with vanilla extract, nut‑derived aromatics, or a buttery note.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Like any non‑alcoholic drink, cream soda contributes to the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Contains simple sugars that are rapidly absorbed, providing an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Culinary enhancer
items.content: Used in cooking to add sweetness and light carbonation to desserts and sauces.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption can lead to weight gain, tooth decay, and elevated blood glucose levels.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature may irritate the stomach in people with sensitivity.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some versions are flavored with nut or dairy extracts, which may trigger allergies.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink cream soda chilled, use it in cocktail mixes, add to ice cream, fruit salads, or incorporate into pancake batter for a light, airy texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3‑5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Vegetable tempura is a Japanese dish consisting of bite‑size pieces of vegetables coated in a light batter made from flour, starch, egg and cold water, then deep‑fried. The result is a crisp, airy crust that keeps the natural flavor and tenderness of vegetables such as bell pepper, eggplant, broccoli, carrot and pumpkin.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tempura was introduced to Japan in the 16th century by Portuguese missionaries.
The batter is kept cold, sometimes with ice, to create a light, airy coating.
Rice flour or corn starch is often added to the batter for extra crunch.
Vegetable tempura is commonly served with soy sauce, teriyaki, or a special tempura dipping sauce (tentsuyu).
In Japan, a “tempura‑zen” platter includes a variety of vegetables and seafood.

items.title: Rich source of vegetables
items.content: Tempura retains most of the vitamins and minerals of the original vegetables, such as vitamin C, beta‑carotene and potassium.

items.title: Low in fat when prepared correctly
items.content: When fried quickly in a small amount of oil, tempura remains relatively low‑calorie compared with other fried foods.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The vegetables provide fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Vitamins and phytochemicals in the vegetables help combat free radicals.

items.title: Natural glutamates
items.content: Some vegetables, like tomatoes and mushrooms, contain natural glutamate that enhances flavor without added MSG.

items.title: Seafood cross‑contamination
items.content: Even vegetable tempura is often fried in the same oil as seafood, which can be a problem for people with shellfish allergies.

items.title: Oil temperature
items.content: Maintaining the correct frying temperature (170‑180 °C) is essential; too low a temperature makes the batter absorb excess oil.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Dipping sauces are usually salty; those monitoring sodium should choose low‑salt versions.

items.title: Potential foodborne hazards
items.content: Use fresh vegetables and clean oil to avoid bacterial contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve tempura hot, typically with soy sauce, teriyaki, or tentsuyu. A light sprinkle of salt or toasted sesame seeds adds flavor. The crispy coating pairs well with a light broth or rice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Tempura is best enjoyed immediately after frying. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 1‑2 days; reheat in the oven to restore crispness.
